## UAE contract‑law issues (delay, non‑conformity, withholding, termination, damages, arbitration)

Below is a practical overview of the UAE law framework that will typically apply to a UAE‑governed equipment supply contract involving late delivery, failed tests, withheld payment, termination and arbitration, focusing on the Civil Transactions Law (Civil Code) and sale‑of‑goods concepts.

1. Legal framework and contract type  
- Equipment supply is generally treated as a contract of sale of movables under the Civil Code (Federal Law No. 5 of 1985, as amended), supplemented by the parties’ contract (specs, tests, milestones, LDs, etc.).  
- Core principles: good faith performance, binding force of contract, freedom of contract subject to mandatory rules.

2. Delay in delivery  
- Supplier must deliver on the contractual delivery date/milestones. Significant delay = breach.  
- Remedies (unless varied by contract):  
  - Demand specific performance and claim delay damages.  
  - Treat serious delay that defeats the purpose as fundamental breach and seek termination plus damages.  
- Contracts often add LDs and long‑stop dates; tribunals usually enforce them but may adjust clearly punitive LDs.

3. Non‑conformity and failed acceptance tests  
- Equipment must meet the agreed specifications and implied fitness for purpose.  
- Contractual FAT/SAT and performance tests are the main mechanism to determine conformity.  
- Failed tests = strong evidence of non‑conformity. Supplier must rectify, repair or replace within reasonable/contractual periods; persistent inability to pass tests may be fundamental breach.  
- Buyer must inspect and notify defects/non‑conformity within a reasonable time; sitting on known defects risks losing rights, especially if behaviour looks like acceptance.  
- UAE law does not adopt a strict “perfect tender” rule, but detailed specs/tests are often treated as strict requirements. Minor, non‑material deviations are more likely to be treated as curable, not termination‑worthy.

4. Withholding / non‑payment  
- In reciprocal contracts, each party’s obligation is conditional on the other’s performance.  
- Buyer can withhold payment where the supplier has not performed or has defective performance, especially the final installment expressly linked to successful acceptance.  
- Withholding must be proportionate: holding back the whole price where performance is largely conforming may be attacked as excessive. Tribunals often order payment of undisputed sums and allow withholding only for disputed parts or security.

5. Termination rights  
- Termination may be:  
  - Contractual: specified triggers (prolonged delay; failure to pass tests within X attempts/time; material breach not cured after notice).  
  - Statutory: Civil Code allows termination (“rescission”) for serious non‑performance.  
- To justify buyer termination, tribunals look at:  
  - Seriousness and persistence of breach (delay + repeated test failures).  
  - Whether the supplier had proper notice and a realistic opportunity to cure.  
  - Impact on the core purpose of the contract.  
- Premature termination, or termination without contractual/required notices and cure periods, risks being treated as wrongful, exposing the buyer to damages.

6. Damages  
- Purpose: put injured party (as money can) in position as if proper performance occurred.  
- Conditions: breach, actual loss, causation, foreseeability.  
- Typical recoverable items in this context:  
  - Direct costs of replacement/rectification, extra installation/engineering.  
  - Delay costs (extended overheads, financing).  
  - Lost profit/loss of use where sufficiently certain and foreseeable (tribunals are conservative).  
  - Contractual liquidated damages (delay/under‑performance LDs), subject to tribunal’s power to reduce or, in some cases, increase them to match actual harm.  
- Mitigation is expected; avoidable or inflated losses may not be fully compensated.

7. “Substantial compliance” / substantial performance  
- Not labelled as such in the Civil Code but recognised in effect:  
  - Where performance is largely complete and usable, and defects are minor and remediable, tribunals often refuse total termination, preferring rectification, price reduction and/or damages.  
  - Where defects go to core performance or safety and cannot be remedied in reasonable time, termination is more likely.  
- Supplier’s “substantial compliance” argument invites the tribunal to:  
  - Reject termination;  
  - Require completion/rectification; and  
  - Award a price adjustment/damages instead of allowing the buyer to avoid the price entirely.

8. Arbitration clause interaction  
- A valid arbitration clause obliges UAE courts to decline jurisdiction over merits if invoked in time. The clause is separable: the tribunal decides on validity, termination and damages of the main contract.  
- Tribunal applies UAE substantive law if chosen: the same Civil Code/Commercial law principles above.  
- Courts support arbitration with interim measures, appointment issues, and enforcement/annulment; they do not re‑decide merits except on narrow public‑policy grounds.  
- Pending arbitration, buyer can usually continue to withhold contested payments in good faith; supplier can seek interim measures or partial awards on undisputed sums.

Applied to your facts:  
- Late delivery + repeated failed tests strongly support buyer’s breach case, if well documented and if notice/cure procedures were followed.  
- Withholding a final payment tied to successful acceptance is consistent with UAE law if acceptance legitimately never occurred; withholding much more than that is riskier.  
- Termination will be judged on seriousness of breach and strictness of compliance with contractual termination steps.  
- “Substantial compliance” will hinge on technical evidence: are defects minor/curable or fundamental?

---

## Arguments, missing evidence/notices, and litigation/arbitration risk

### Core issues and likely contract structure

Issues: late delivery, failure of acceptance tests, withheld final payment, termination, supplier’s “substantial compliance” and threat of arbitration.  
Likely key clauses: delivery/timing and LDs, specs and test regime, warranty/cure, payment milestones and withholding, termination for cause with cure periods, arbitration clause.

### Buyer vs supplier arguments

A. Late delivery  
- Buyer: delivery date was essential; delay is material; LDs (if any) apply; delay plus defects justify withholding and termination.  
- Supplier: delay excused or partly caused by buyer (site readiness, variations, approvals, force majeure); buyer waived strict deadlines by conduct; remedy should be LDs, not termination/non‑payment, unless contract says otherwise.

B. Failed acceptance tests / non‑conformity  
- Buyer: tests contractually defined; failures material; equipment doesn’t meet specs; repeated failures despite cure; buyer entitled to reject, withhold, and terminate.  
- Supplier: tests not run per protocol; environment/operation at site caused failures; defects minor/curable; substantial performance achieved; buyer obstructed testing or cure; continued buyer use = acceptance/waiver.

C. Withheld final payment  
- Buyer: final milestone expressly conditional on acceptance; condition not met; buyer may withhold and set‑off damages; payment now would undermine leverage.  
- Supplier: conditions substantially met; only minor issues remain; buyer’s total withholding is abusive and itself a breach; buyer benefits from equipment and must pay at least the undisputed part.

D. Termination  
- Buyer: contract allows termination for prolonged delay and/or repeated failed tests/material breach; required notices and cure periods were served and ignored; termination proportionate given impact.  
- Supplier: termination invalid; notice/cure steps not followed; breaches not “material” or were curable; buyer should have used LDs and repair remedies; wrongful termination gives supplier claims for price, demobilisation and lost profit.

### Missing / critical evidence and notices

What you need to assemble:

1) Contract & annexes  
- Full contract, including: delivery schedule; LDs; detailed specs; test/acceptance mechanism; warranty and cure; payment milestones; withholding/set‑off rights; termination for cause; notice requirements; dispute resolution/arbitration clause; amendments/variation orders.

2) Chronology & notices  
- Agreed vs actual delivery dates.  
- Test dates and outcomes.  
- Delay notices, EOT claims and responses.  
- Non‑conformity/test‑failure notices.  
- Formal default/cure notices and termination notice (content, timing, service method).

3) Technical/testing record  
- Test procedures and acceptance criteria.  
- FAT/SAT reports (pass/fail, partial passes, re‑tests).  
- Root‑cause analysis, site conditions.  
- Independent expert reports on severity and curability of defects.

4) Payment & financials  
- Invoices, payment certificates; amount and portion of price withheld.  
- Any set‑off notices and LD calculations.  
- Buyer’s replacement or remedial contracts (if any) and costs.

5) Use/benefit  
- Evidence of buyer’s use/operation of the equipment pre‑ and post‑termination.  
- Any taking‑over/provisional acceptance documents.

Notice gaps on the buyer side (no or defective default/termination notices) can severely damage the termination case. Weak technical documentation undermines both parties’ claims.

### Risk assessment

Buyer – main risks  
- Wrongful withholding: if final payment is wholly withheld despite substantial performance, tribunal may order payment of all or most of it plus interest/costs, allowing only limited set‑off.  
- Wrongful termination: if contractual preconditions (notice/cure) weren’t met or defects/delays are found remediable and not fundamental, termination can be held wrongful, exposing buyer to supplier’s damages (unpaid price, lost profit, wasted costs).  
- Weak record: missing or informal notices, poorly documented tests and losses weaken case and encourage adverse inference.

Supplier – main risks  
- Liability for late delivery: if buyer‑caused delay/force majeure is not convincingly shown, supplier faces LDs or delay damages.  
- Non‑conformity: clear, repeated failures of core performance/safety tests and inability to cure support buyer’s non‑conformity and termination position, at least for part of the contract.  
- Termination upheld: if breaches are serious and persistent, and buyer’s notices/cure steps are solid, tribunal may uphold termination and award buyer replacement and delay costs.  
- Partial recovery only: tribunal may find substantial performance and grant price minus significant deductions/LDs and remedial costs.

Likely tribunal approach  
- Distinguish core defects (capacity, safety, regulatory compliance) from minor issues: only the former justify termination.  
- Critically examine notice and cure steps: if buyer has not complied, supplier gains leverage.  
- Favour financial adjustments over contract “wipe‑out” where performance is largely usable.  
- Encourage or reflect a middle‑ground outcome: partial payment of price plus some damages/discounts.

### Settlement positions and structures

Given mutual risk and arbitration cost, the rational “zone” is usually a compromise around netting out unpaid price vs. credible delay/defect claims.

For buyer  
- Accept that some payment is likely due if equipment is substantially usable.  
- Seek:  
  - Price discount reflecting delay and defects (via LDs or lump sum).  
  - Supplier‑funded remedial programme with clear tests and time frames.  
  - Retention or extended warranty instead of total non‑payment.  
- Convert termination into a negotiated “mutual termination and settlement” with:  
  - Agreed final status;  
  - Clear allocation of remedial responsibilities;  
  - Mutual releases.

For supplier  
- Acknowledge delay/defect exposure; all‑or‑nothing stance is risky.  
- Offer:  
  - Reasonable discount or LD credit against immediate release of most withheld sums.  
  - Defined remedial plan with milestone‑based payments.  
  - If relationship is unsalvageable, accept partial payment and mutual walk‑away, possibly recovering or reselling equipment where practicable.

Common structures  
- Price haircut + release: buyer pays, for example, 50–80% of withheld amount; both sides waive further claims.  
- Completion and staged payment: partial immediate payment, balance released on successful re‑tests, with retention.  
- Netting: agree a quantified schedule of defects/delay and net against price; pay the net in full and final settlement.  
- Structured exit: buyer keeps equipment at a discount; supplier waives balance and warranties may or may not survive, depending on risk allocation.

## Draft improved clauses (inspection, testing, acceptance, withholding, termination – UAE‑governed equipment supply)

INSPECTION, TESTING, ACCEPTANCE, WITHHOLDING AND TERMINATION FOR CAUSE

1. Definitions  

1.1 In this Agreement, and in this Clause:

(a) “Equipment” means the equipment, materials, components, software (if any), and associated documentation to be supplied by the Supplier under this Agreement, as further described in the Specifications.  

(b) “Specifications” means the technical specifications, performance criteria, functional requirements, drawings, standards, and any other requirements expressly set out in this Agreement, its schedules and annexes, and any agreed written variations thereto.  

(c) “Delivery Date” means the date or dates for delivery of the Equipment as specified in this Agreement, as may be amended in accordance with its terms.  

(d) “Inspection” means the review, examination and verification activities carried out by or on behalf of the Buyer to determine whether the Equipment conforms to the Specifications and the Agreement, including visual inspection, document review and such other checks as the Buyer reasonably deems necessary.  

(e) “Tests” or “Acceptance Tests” means the tests, trials and demonstrations described in this Agreement and/or the Specifications, to be carried out to determine whether the Equipment meets the Specifications, including performance, reliability, safety and integration requirements.  

(f) “Acceptance” means the Buyer’s written confirmation that the Equipment has successfully passed all required Inspections and Acceptance Tests and meets all applicable requirements of this Agreement, subject only to any minor defects expressly agreed in writing by the Buyer to be remedied after Acceptance.  

(g) “Substantial Compliance” or “Substantial Performance” means, for the purposes of this Agreement only, performance that meets all material requirements of the Specifications and this Agreement so that the Equipment is fully fit for its intended purpose, with only minor defects which do not affect safety, functionality, performance, reliability, serviceability, or integration with the Buyer’s systems, and which can be remedied without material disruption to the Buyer’s operations. The existence of any material non‑conformity shall exclude any claim by the Supplier of Substantial Compliance or Substantial Performance.  

(h) “Non‑Conformity” means any failure of the Equipment to comply with the Specifications, this Agreement, applicable law, good industry practice, or any failure to successfully pass any Inspection or Acceptance Test.  

(i) “Cure Period” has the meaning given in Clause 6.3 below.

2. Inspection and Testing  

2.1 Right to Inspect and Witness Tests  

(a) The Buyer, its employees, agents, and/or representatives shall have the right, but not the obligation, to:  
  (i) inspect the Equipment, any components, and related documentation at the Supplier’s premises, at the premises of any sub‑supplier, and/or at the Delivery Location; and  
  (ii) witness any factory tests, pre‑shipment tests, site tests, commissioning tests, and Acceptance Tests,  

in each case upon reasonable prior notice and during normal working hours, provided that such activities do not unreasonably disrupt the Supplier’s operations.  

(b) The Supplier shall provide the Buyer with all reasonable assistance, access, information, and documentation requested for the purposes of Inspection and witnessing tests, including test procedures, test plans, test records, and calibration certificates.

2.2 Test Procedures, Criteria and Schedule  

(a) The parties shall agree in writing, prior to commencement of any Acceptance Test, the detailed test procedures, acceptance criteria, and test schedule, consistent with the Specifications and the provisions of this Agreement. In the event of any inconsistency, the stricter or more demanding requirement shall apply, unless the parties expressly agree otherwise in writing.  

(b) The Supplier shall give the Buyer not less than [●] Business Days’ prior written notice of the date on which any Test(s) will be carried out, and shall not proceed with any Test that the Buyer has reasonably requested be rescheduled, provided that such rescheduling does not result in an unreasonable delay.

2.3 Costs of Testing  

(a) The Supplier shall bear all costs of Inspections and Tests conducted at its own or its sub‑suppliers’ premises, including provision of necessary equipment, materials, consumables, utilities and personnel.  

(b) The Supplier shall bear all costs of any re‑tests required due to Non‑Conformity or failure to pass any Test. If the Buyer incurs any reasonable additional costs as a direct result of such re‑tests (including travel and accommodation of its representatives), the Supplier shall reimburse those costs upon presentation of reasonable supporting documentation.

3. Delivery, Late Delivery and Consequences  

3.1 Timely Delivery  

(a) Time for delivery of the Equipment in accordance with the Delivery Date(s) is of the essence of this Agreement.  

(b) The Supplier shall deliver the Equipment in accordance with the agreed Incoterms, Delivery Date(s), and any delivery requirements set out in this Agreement.

3.2 Notice of Delay  

(a) The Supplier shall promptly notify the Buyer in writing as soon as it becomes aware of any circumstance likely to cause a delay in delivery or completion of Tests or Acceptance. Such notice shall set out:  
  (i) the cause of the delay;  
  (ii) the expected duration of the delay; and  
  (iii) proposed measures to mitigate the delay.  

(b) The giving of such notice shall not relieve the Supplier of any of its obligations or liabilities under this Agreement, nor shall it constitute a waiver by the Buyer of any rights or remedies.

3.3 Consequences of Late Delivery  

(a) Without prejudice to any other rights or remedies of the Buyer (including liquidated damages, if provided elsewhere in this Agreement), if the Supplier fails to deliver the Equipment by the relevant Delivery Date, the Buyer shall be entitled, at its option, to:  
  (i) accept late delivery, subject to any applicable liquidated damages or other remedies; and/or  
  (ii) withhold any payments linked to delivery and/or Acceptance until such time as full delivery and Acceptance are achieved; and/or  
  (iii) treat such delay as a material breach for the purpose of termination under Clause 7, if the delay exceeds [●] days or such other period as may be specified in this Agreement.

4. Acceptance Procedure  

4.1 Delivery, Installation and Commissioning  

(a) Upon delivery of the Equipment to the Delivery Location, the Supplier shall, where applicable, install and commission the Equipment in accordance with the Agreement, the Specifications, and good industry practice.  

(b) The Supplier shall notify the Buyer in writing when the Equipment is ready for Acceptance Testing.

4.2 Conduct of Acceptance Tests  

(a) The Buyer shall commence Acceptance Tests within [●] Business Days after receipt of the Supplier’s notice under Clause 4.1(b), or such other period as the parties may agree in writing.  

(b) Acceptance Tests shall be conducted in accordance with the agreed test procedures and criteria. The Buyer may, acting reasonably, require additional or extended tests where necessary to confirm compliance with the Specifications or to verify the rectification of any Non‑Conformity.

4.3 Acceptance or Rejection  

(a) Within [●] Business Days after completion of the Acceptance Tests, the Buyer shall notify the Supplier in writing of:  
  (i) its Acceptance of the Equipment; or  
  (ii) its rejection of the Equipment, specifying in reasonable detail any Non‑Conformities identified.  

(b) If the Buyer does not issue a notification within the period referred to in Clause 4.3(a), and provided that:  
  (i) the Supplier has given written notice that the Equipment is ready for Acceptance Testing; and  
  (ii) the Buyer has had a reasonable opportunity to perform Acceptance Tests; and  
  (iii) there are no unresolved Non‑Conformities previously notified by the Buyer;  
then the Equipment shall not be deemed accepted solely by reason of the passage of time, but the Supplier may request in writing that the Buyer promptly complete the Acceptance Tests. The parties shall then agree a short, reasonable period within which such Tests shall be completed. Any deemed acceptance must be expressly agreed in writing by the Buyer; silence or non‑response shall not constitute Acceptance.

4.4 Effect of Acceptance; No Waiver of Latent Defects  

(a) Acceptance of the Equipment confirms only that, at the time of Acceptance, the Equipment met the Acceptance criteria then tested. Acceptance does not:  
  (i) constitute a waiver of any latent or hidden defects; or  
  (ii) limit or exclude the Supplier’s obligations or liabilities under warranties, guarantees, or other provisions of this Agreement.  

(b) The Buyer shall be entitled to notify the Supplier of any latent or hidden Non‑Conformity discovered after Acceptance and to require the Supplier to remedy such Non‑Conformity in accordance with the warranty provisions of this Agreement.

5. Substantial Compliance and Non‑Conformities  

5.1 Substantial Compliance  

(a) The Supplier acknowledges and agrees that:  
  (i) “Substantial Compliance” or “Substantial Performance” shall have the limited meaning set out in Clause 1.1(g); and  
  (ii) any decision as to whether the Equipment meets the threshold of Substantial Compliance shall be made by the Buyer acting reasonably and in good faith, having regard to the Specifications and the intended purpose of the Equipment.  

(b) For avoidance of doubt, the Supplier shall not be entitled to claim that the Buyer is obliged to accept the Equipment solely on the basis of partial, incomplete or approximate performance, or on grounds of Substantial Compliance, where:  
  (i) the Equipment does not fully meet all material requirements of the Specifications; or  
  (ii) the Equipment fails any material Acceptance Test; or  
  (iii) any Non‑Conformity adversely affects safety, functionality, performance, reliability, compatibility or regulatory compliance.

5.2 Minor Defects  

(a) The Buyer may, but is not obliged to, grant Acceptance subject to the Supplier’s written agreement to remedy minor defects within a specified time. Minor defects are those that:  
  (i) do not affect safety;  
  (ii) do not materially affect functionality, performance, or reliability; and  
  (iii) can be remedied without material impact on the Buyer’s operations.  

(b) Any list of minor defects and their agreed rectification period shall be set out in an agreed punch list signed by both parties. The Supplier shall promptly remedy all such minor defects at its own cost within the period specified, failing which the Buyer may exercise its rights under Clauses 5.3 and 7.

5.3 Failed Tests and Repeated Non‑Conformities  

(a) If the Equipment fails any Acceptance Test or is otherwise found to be Non‑Conforming, the Buyer may reject the Equipment in whole or in part and require the Supplier, at the Supplier’s sole cost and risk and within a time period reasonably specified by the Buyer, to:  
  (i) promptly remedy the Non‑Conformity; and/or  
  (ii) replace the Non‑Conforming Equipment with new conforming equipment; and/or  
  (iii) repeat the relevant Tests after correction or replacement.  

(b) If, after the Supplier’s remedial efforts, the Equipment again fails any Acceptance Test, or if the Supplier fails to remedy the Non‑Conformity within the specified time:  
  (i) the Buyer may, at its sole discretion and without prejudice to any other rights and remedies, elect one or more of the following:  
    (A) allow the Supplier a further opportunity to remedy the Non‑Conformity under a revised timetable agreed in writing; or  
    (B) procure alternative equipment and/or services from a third party and recover from the Supplier all additional direct costs reasonably incurred by the Buyer as a result; or  
    (C) reject the Equipment in whole or in part and terminate this Agreement, in whole or in part, for cause under Clause 7; and  
  (ii) the Supplier shall refund to the Buyer all amounts paid in respect of any rejected Equipment, together with any associated charges, within [●] days of the Buyer’s written demand.

6. Withholding of Payments  

6.1 Milestone‑Linked Payments  

(a) Where payments are linked to delivery milestones, completion of Tests, and/or Acceptance, the Supplier acknowledges that the Buyer is under no obligation to make such payments unless and until the relevant milestone has been properly achieved and documented.  

(b) The Supplier shall submit invoices only for milestones that have been achieved in accordance with this Agreement. The Buyer shall be entitled to reject any invoice that does not correspond to an achieved milestone.

6.2 Right to Withhold  

(a) Without prejudice to any other rights or remedies, the Buyer may withhold payment of any portion of the Contract Price which corresponds to:  
  (i) Equipment that has not been delivered in accordance with this Agreement;  
  (ii) Equipment that has not been Accepted in accordance with Clause 4;  
  (iii) portions of work or Equipment affected by a notified Non‑Conformity;  
  (iv) any amounts reasonably disputed by the Buyer in good faith; or  
  (v) any amounts that the Buyer is entitled to set off under this Agreement.  

(b) The Buyer shall notify the Supplier in writing of its reasons for withholding any payment, and, to the extent reasonably practicable, the amount so withheld shall be proportionate to the value of the Non‑Conforming or undelivered Equipment or the disputed amount.

6.3 Cure of Non‑Conformity and Release of Withheld Amounts  

(a) Where payment has been withheld due to Non‑Conformity or failure to achieve a milestone, the Supplier shall remedy the cause of withholding within a period to be specified by the Buyer in writing (the “Cure Period”), taking into account the nature and seriousness of the issue.  

(b) Once the Supplier has remedied the Non‑Conformity and the Equipment has successfully passed any required re‑Tests and/or has been Accepted, the Buyer shall pay any withheld amounts that are no longer in dispute within [●] days, subject always to:  
  (i) the Buyer’s right of set‑off against any sums due to the Buyer from the Supplier; and  
  (ii) any other rights and remedies that the Buyer may have under this Agreement or at law.  

(c) The Supplier acknowledges that the Buyer’s withholding of payment in accordance with this Clause 6 shall not constitute a breach of this Agreement, nor entitle the Supplier to suspend performance or to terminate this Agreement, provided that the Buyer acts in good faith.

7. Termination for Cause  

7.1 Buyer’s Right to Terminate for Cause  

Without prejudice to any other rights or remedies available under this Agreement, at law or in equity, the Buyer may, by written notice to the Supplier, terminate this Agreement in whole or in part with immediate effect (or with effect from such date as the Buyer may specify in the notice) upon the occurrence of any of the following events:

(a) Material Delay:  
The Supplier fails to deliver the Equipment, or any material portion thereof, within [●] days after the applicable Delivery Date, or fails to achieve Acceptance within [●] days after the date originally scheduled for Acceptance, other than due to a force majeure event duly notified in accordance with this Agreement.

(b) Repeated Failure of Tests:  
The Equipment fails any material Acceptance Test on [●] or more occasions, or repeated Non‑Conformities occur which, in the reasonable opinion of the Buyer, indicate that the Supplier is unable or unwilling to provide conforming Equipment within a reasonable time.

(c) Failure to Remedy:  
The Supplier fails to remedy any Non‑Conformity or other material breach relating to delivery, quality, performance, or Testing of the Equipment within the applicable Cure Period specified in a written notice from the Buyer.

(d) Persistent Breach:  
The Supplier commits repeated, persistent or systemic breaches of its obligations under this Agreement (whether or not remedied) which, taken together, materially impair the achievement of the purpose of this Agreement or the Buyer’s ability to use the Equipment as intended.

(e) Insolvency or Similar Events:  
Any insolvency, bankruptcy, liquidation, or comparable event occurs in respect of the Supplier, as further described in the general termination provisions of this Agreement.

7.2 Procedure and Consequences of Termination for Cause  

(a) The Buyer shall notify the Supplier in writing of its decision to terminate under Clause 7.1, specifying the grounds for termination and the effective date of termination.  

(b) Upon termination for cause pursuant to this Clause 7:  
  (i) the Supplier shall immediately cease all affected work and shall take all necessary steps to protect and preserve the Equipment, materials and any items belonging to the Buyer;  
  (ii) the Buyer may take over any partially completed Equipment, materials, documentation, and work‑in‑progress, and may use them to complete the project itself or to have a third party do so; and  
  (iii) the Supplier shall promptly refund to the Buyer all amounts paid in respect of Equipment which has not been delivered and Accepted in accordance with this Agreement, together with any other amounts refundable under this Agreement.  

(c) The Buyer shall be entitled to recover from the Supplier all direct additional costs and expenses reasonably incurred by the Buyer in procuring substitute equipment and/or services from a third party as a result of such termination, subject to any agreed limitations of liability under this Agreement.

7.3 Effect on Substantial Compliance Claims  

(a) Termination by the Buyer under this Clause 7 shall not be affected by, nor conditional upon, any claim by the Supplier that it has achieved Substantial Compliance or Substantial Performance.  

(b) Any dispute as to whether the Supplier has achieved Substantial Compliance or Substantial Performance shall not limit or delay the Buyer’s right to terminate under this Clause 7, provided that the Buyer has acted reasonably and in good faith in assessing the Supplier’s performance.

8. Reservation of Rights  

8.1 The rights and remedies of the Buyer under this Clause are cumulative and are in addition to, and not in substitution for, any other rights or remedies available to the Buyer under this Agreement, under applicable law (including the laws of the United Arab Emirates), or otherwise.  

8.2 No failure or delay by the Buyer in exercising any right, power or remedy shall operate as a waiver thereof, nor shall any single or partial exercise of any such right, power or remedy preclude any other or further exercise thereof or the exercise of any other right, power or remedy.

Below is a structured comparison and risk assessment based on UAE‑law style principles for sale/supply of goods and typical equipment contracts. This is general dispute analysis, not legal advice.

---

## 1. Core Issues & Likely Contract Structure

Typical disputed issues:
- Was delivery late under the contract schedule?
- Did the equipment comply with technical specs and pass acceptance tests?
- Did the buyer give proper notices and opportunities to cure?
- Was the buyer entitled to:
  - withhold final payment, and
  - terminate (for delay and/or failed acceptance)?
- Is the supplier entitled to claim the final price for “substantial compliance”?

Key contract clauses (but not provided):
- Delivery/Time of essence, LDs for delay
- Specs and acceptance test regime
- Defect / warranty / cure provisions
- Payment milestones and right to withhold
- Termination for cause (material breach, cure periods)
- Dispute resolution (arbitration clause, seat, rules)

---

## 2. Buyer vs Supplier – Main Arguments

### A. Late delivery

**Buyer arguments**
- Contract delivery date(s) missed; time is of the essence.
- Delay is material: impacts operations, liquidated damages may apply.
- Delay plus non‑conformity justifies termination and withholding final payment.

**Supplier counterarguments**
- Delays excused: variations, late approvals, site readiness, force majeure, or buyer’s conduct.
- Buyer waived strict dates via conduct (accepting revised schedules, using the equipment).
- Even if late, remedy is LDs, not termination or price withholding, unless contract says otherwise.

**Evidence needed**
- Final agreed delivery schedule(s) and any amendments.
- Correspondence on delays, extensions, causes.
- Any LD notices or reservations of rights.

---

### B. Failed acceptance tests / non‑conformity

**Buyer arguments**
- Acceptance tests defined in contract; equipment failed specific tests.
- Non‑conformity is material: equipment cannot meet operational requirements.
- Proper rejection/notice given; supplier failed to remedy within agreed time.
- Under UAE‑style principles, buyer can reject, demand replacement/repair, or terminate for serious non‑conformity.

**Supplier counterarguments**
- Tests improperly conducted / not according to protocol or standards.
- Failures are minor and curable; equipment is substantially compliant.
- Buyer obstructed testing or refused reasonable corrective actions.
- Buyer’s continued use of equipment amounts to acceptance or waiver.
- Right to cure under the contract and general principles: buyer terminated prematurely.

**Evidence needed**
- Contract test procedures, performance criteria, and acceptance mechanism.
- Test reports (including any passed/failed criteria, re‑tests).
- Technical expert reports on seriousness of deviations.
- Emails/minutes documenting proposed remedial works and buyer’s responses.

---

### C. Withholding final payment

**Buyer justification**
- Final milestone is typically upon successful acceptance; condition precedent not met.
- Under commercial practice, buyer may suspend/withhold payment for defective/ incomplete performance.
- Payment now would undermine leverage to enforce remedy.

**Supplier position**
- Preconditions for final payment are satisfied or substantially satisfied (e.g., only minor defects pending).
- Buyer’s withholding is abusive / bad‑faith and itself a breach.
- Even where defects exist, buyer may be limited to warranty/cure and LDs, not complete non‑payment.
- If buyer derives benefit (uses equipment), price should be paid subject to deductions.

**Evidence needed**
- Payment terms and preconditions for the final milestone.
- Any interim certificates, provisional acceptance, or “taking‑over” documents.
- Invoices and buyer’s written reasons for non‑payment.

---

### D. Termination

**Buyer justification**
- Contract allows termination for:
  - prolonged delay beyond specified limit; and/or
  - failure to pass acceptance tests within cure period; or
  - material breach not cured after notice.
- Buyer issued formal notice(s) specifying breaches and cure period; supplier failed.
- Termination is proportionate given delay + failure + business impact.

**Supplier counterarguments**
- Contractual preconditions to termination not met:
  - no valid default notice,
  - insufficient cure period,
  - termination notice defective in form or manner.
- Breaches not “material” or were substantially cured; termination is itself wrongful.
- Buyer should have pursued agreed remedies (LDs, repair, replacement) instead.

**Evidence needed**
- Default notices, cure notices, termination notice(s) with dates and method of service.
- Evidence supplier was given (or not given) a realistic opportunity to cure.
- Internal decision records showing reasons and timing for termination.

---

## 3. Missing Evidence / Notice Gaps (Both Sides)

Currently missing/uncertain:
- Full contract (all clauses listed above).
- Detailed chronology: PO, agreed delivery date, actual delivery, test dates, notice dates, termination date.
- Written notices:
  - delay notices,
  - non‑conformity / test‑failure notices,
  - cure demands,
  - termination notice.
- Any minutes or emails showing:
  - agreement on revised dates,
  - acceptance or rejection of remedial proposals.
- Proof of use/benefit of the equipment post‑delivery.
- Any LD calculations or set‑off notices.

Notice defects could be critical. If the buyer:
- only complained informally, or
- never gave a proper cure notice,
its right to terminate/withhold may be undermined.

If the supplier:
- failed to respond substantively,
- missed cure commitments,
its plea of substantial compliance weakens.

---

## 4. Risk Assessment – Buyer

**Strengths**
- Clear failed acceptance tests (if well‑documented).
- Clear, significant delay with impact on operations.
- Contract conditions clearly link final payment to successful acceptance.
- Compliant notices and cure opportunities.

**Risks / Weaknesses**
- Inadequate or late notices; no formal cure opportunity.
- Acceptance by conduct (using equipment, signing any “taking‑over” certificate).
- Non‑conformities are minor or easily curable; termination may appear disproportionate.
- If contract restricts withholding to limited situations, buyer’s non‑payment may be treated as breach.
- Arbitration clause may require pre‑steps (negotiation, mediation); skipping them may cause procedural objections.

Strategically, buyer’s leverage:
- Physical possession of equipment.
- Ability to document technical failures and operational losses.
But this is offset by:
- Exposure to claim for unpaid price, LD‑limited delay, and damages for wrongful termination.

---

## 5. Risk Assessment – Supplier

**Strengths**
- Any evidence of substantial performance and operational use of equipment.
- Contract language limiting termination to very specific triggers or requiring strict notice.
- Evidence of buyer’s obstructive or inconsistent behavior (moving goalposts on specs/tests).

**Risks / Weaknesses**
- Clear, repeated test failures on core performance criteria.
- Significant, unjustified delay with documented buyer complaints.
- Poor documentation of remedial efforts or non‑attendance at tests.
- If contract explicitly allows withholding/termination for failed acceptance, difficult to compel payment without curing.

Procedurally, the supplier initiating arbitration:
- Gains initiative and forum for technical expert evidence.
- But risks a counterclaim for costs, delay damages, and replacement expenses if performance is found non‑conforming.

---

## 6. Strategic Considerations / Pressure Points

For the **buyer**:
- Strengthen file: ensure all test reports, technical opinions, and notices are organized and consistent.
- Quantify losses and delay impact; quantify LDs and any cost to rectify or replace.
- Evaluate whether partial payment against firm remedial commitments could be a commercially safer settlement than all‑or‑nothing litigation.

For the **supplier**:
- Gather strong technical evidence that:
  - tests were improperly run, and/or
  - non‑conformities are minor and already cured or easily curable.
- Highlight any contractual/formal defects in buyer’s notices and termination.
- Offer pragmatic remedial measures (upgrades, extended warranty, price reductions) to de‑risk an arbitration focused on technical failings and notice compliance.

If you’d like, I can:
- Work through a specific timeline you provide, or
- Review the contract (or key clauses) to refine the risk assessment for each side.

Below is a practical overview of the **UAE law framework** that will typically apply to a UAE‑governed equipment supply contract involving late delivery, failed tests, withheld payment, termination and arbitration. I’ll focus on the *Civil Transactions Law* (UAE Civil Code) and general sale‑of‑goods principles, not on court procedure.

> **Important:** Article numbers and headings can vary between consolidated translations. For anything contentious or high‑value you should cross‑check the precise Arabic text and your contract wording and obtain UAE‑qualified advice.

---

## 1. Legal framework for an equipment supply contract

A UAE‑governed equipment supply contract is generally treated as:

- a **contract of sale** (movable goods) under the UAE Civil Transactions Law (Federal Law No. 5 of 1985 as amended), plus  
- specific **contractual terms** agreed by the parties (INCOTERMS, milestones, testing regime, liquidated damages etc.).

Key Civil Code concepts that will usually be relevant:

- **Good faith performance** (parties must perform in good faith).
- **Binding force of contract** (contract is the law between the parties).
- **Freedom of contract**, subject to mandatory rules and public order.
- Rules on **delay**, **non‑conformity**, **rescission/termination**, **damages** and **arbitration agreements**.

---

## 2. Delay in delivery

### a) Basic rule: obligation to perform on time

Under the Civil Code, a debtor (supplier) must perform as agreed. If a date is fixed, performance should be on that date. Delay occurs when:

- the supplier fails to deliver on the **contractual delivery date**, or  
- fails to achieve a **time‑critical milestone** (e.g., FAT/SAT or completion date) that is clearly tied to performance.

Unless the contract clearly makes time “not of the essence”, significant delay in a supply project can amount to **breach**.

### b) Remedies for delay (unless contract says otherwise)

UAE law generally gives the creditor (buyer) the option, in case of serious breach/delay:

- to **insist on performance** (specific performance), possibly with compensation for late performance; or  
- to **seek termination (rescission)** if delay is sufficiently serious and defeats the purpose of the contract; and  
- to **claim damages** for losses caused by the delay (see Section 6).

The contract will often refine this via:

- **liquidated delay damages** (daily/weekly LDs, possibly with a cap); and/or  
- a **grace period** or cure period before termination.

UAE courts/arbitral tribunals will usually respect such clauses **unless** they violate mandatory law or public policy (e.g. manifestly punitive LDs may be reduced).

---

## 3. Non‑conformity and failed acceptance tests

Equipment must conform to:

- **contract specifications** (technical description, performance criteria), and  
- any **implied requirements** for ordinary use, if the contract is silent.

In engineering/equipment contracts, the **acceptance testing regime** (FAT/SAT, performance tests) becomes the concrete mechanism for assessing conformity.

### a) Failure of acceptance tests

If the equipment fails contractual acceptance tests:

- legally, this is strong evidence of **non‑conformity** / defective performance;  
- the supplier is typically obligated to **rectify**, **repair**, or **replace** within a reasonable or contractually specified period;  
- repeated failure or inability to pass tests within agreed time frames can amount to **fundamental breach**, permitting termination.

### b) Buyer obligations on inspection/notification

UAE sale‑of‑goods principles expect the buyer to:

- **inspect** the goods within a reasonable time (or as per contractual test procedures); and  
- **notify** the supplier of defects/non‑conformity within a reasonable time after discovery.

If the buyer sits on known defects for too long without protest, they may lose some rights, especially if they appear to have **accepted** the goods.

### c) “Substantial compliance” vs strict compliance

UAE law does not expressly adopt a “perfect tender” rule like some common‑law systems, but:

- where specifications and tests are detailed, tribunals often treat them as **strict requirements**;  
- minor deviations that do not affect functionality or agreed performance may be treated as **non‑fundamental** and remedied, not as grounds to terminate.

Whether the supplier’s “substantial compliance” argument is accepted will depend heavily on:

- how the acceptance criteria are drafted, and  
- whether the defects materially impair the purpose of the contract or the buyer’s use of the equipment.

---

## 4. Withholding / non‑payment by buyer

### a) General right of retention

Under Civil Code principles of **synallagmatic** (reciprocal) obligations:

- each party’s obligation is generally **conditional** on the other’s performance;  
- a buyer can often **withhold payment** if the seller has **not performed** or has **defective performance**, especially for the unpaid **final/acceptance‑linked installment**.

In practice:

- withholding the **final payment** that is expressly tied to **successful completion/acceptance** is broadly consistent with UAE law if acceptance has not occurred;  
- withholding earlier milestones that have been properly achieved may expose the buyer to default and damages.

### b) Limits and risks

The buyer should avoid withholding more than is reasonably tied to:

- the unperformed or defective part of the obligations; and  
- any amounts expressly stated in the contract to be contingent on **acceptance** or **completion**.

Arbitral tribunals may view **total non‑payment** (including for clearly conforming parts) as disproportionate and may:

- order payment of undisputed sums, and  
- allow withholding only for the disputed part or as security for claims.

Careful **reservation of rights** and contemporaneous notices (linking withheld payment to specific failures/delays) are important.

---

## 5. Termination rights under UAE law

### a) Contractual vs statutory termination

UAE law recognises both:

1. **Contractual termination**:  
   – Most supply contracts specify termination for:
   - prolonged delay,
   - failure to pass tests after x attempts or within y days,  
   - material breach not cured within a certain period.  
   – Tribunals will generally enforce such clauses.

2. **Statutory termination (rescission)**:  
   – The Civil Code gives a party the right, in case of **serious/essential breach**, to request termination, usually via court or agreed dispute forum (e.g. arbitration).  
   – If a **material obligation** is not performed, the innocent party can seek either:
     - compulsive performance, or  
     - termination with damages.

The more clearly your contract defines what constitutes a **fundamental/material breach** (e.g. failure to achieve acceptance by a long‑stop date), the easier it is to justify termination.

### b) Requirements for buyer termination for breach

Key factors a tribunal will look at:

- **Seriousness** of the breach:  
  – prolonged delay;  
  – repeated failed tests;  
  – inability to remedy within reasonable or contractual cure periods.

- **Cure opportunities**:  
  – was the supplier given reasonable notice and an opportunity to fix?  
  – did the contract require a formal default notice / cure period before termination?

- **Causation and impact**:  
  – does the breach substantially deprive the buyer of the benefit of the contract?

A buyer that **terminates prematurely**, when the breach is not yet “fundamental” or when it has not complied with contractual notice/cure procedures, risks being found in **wrongful termination**, and could be liable for the supplier’s damages.

### c) Effect of termination

Upon lawful termination:

- each party is restored as far as possible to the **pre‑contract position**, subject to:
  - retention of amounts corresponding to benefit actually received, and  
  - damages for the breach.

In practice, in supply contracts tribunals typically:

- quantify the value of equipment/services actually usable by the buyer;  
- deduct that from the contract price;  
- then assess damages for delay/non‑conformity or for the costs of replacement / completion by a third party.

---

## 6. Damages under UAE law

### a) General principle

Under the Civil Code:

- Damages are awarded to put the injured party, **as far as money can**, in the position they would have been in had the contract been properly performed.
- The injured party must show:
  1. **Breach**;  
  2. **Actual loss** (material or moral, though commercial matters are usually material loss);  
  3. **Causation**;  
  4. **Foreseeability** (loss that is a normal consequence of the breach or was contemplated at the time of contracting).

### b) Types of losses typically recoverable

In an equipment supply context, this can include:

- **Direct costs**:
  - cost of replacement equipment or rectification;  
  - additional installation/commissioning costs;  
  - extra supervision/engineering costs.

- **Delay‑related**:
  - additional financing costs;  
  - costs from extended site overheads.

- **Loss of use / loss of profit**:
  - under UAE law, **loss of profit** can be compensable if it is reasonably certain and foreseeable (e.g. lost production attributable to the delayed equipment), though tribunals may be conservative.

- **Liquidated damages**:
  - if the contract includes LDs for delay or underperformance, UAE law typically respects them but allows **judicial/arbitral adjustment**:  
    - reduce them if they are clearly excessive compared to actual harm; or  
    - increase them up to the proven actual harm if they are manifestly inadequate (depending on wording and circumstances).

### c) Duty to mitigate

While not always labelled explicitly, UAE tribunals expect the injured party to take **reasonable steps to mitigate** its loss. Excessive or avoidable losses may not be fully recoverable.

---

## 7. Interaction with an arbitration clause

### a) Validity and effect of arbitration clauses

If the contract contains an arbitration clause (e.g. DIAC, ICC, ADCCAC, DIFC‑LCIA, etc.):

- UAE law (including the UAE Arbitration Law and Civil Procedure Code) generally requires courts to **decline jurisdiction** over disputes covered by a valid arbitration agreement, if a party invokes the clause in time;  
- the arbitration clause is usually treated as **separable** from the main contract:  
  – termination or invalidity of the main contract does **not** automatically invalidate the arbitration clause;  
  – the tribunal can decide on **contract validity, termination, and damages**.

### b) What issues an arbitral tribunal can decide

The same UAE substantive law rules described above apply in arbitration, but:

- **procedure and evidence** follow the applicable arbitration rules and the tribunal’s directions, not the UAE Civil Procedure Code (except for matters like enforcement, annulment grounds, etc.);  
- the tribunal can:
  - determine if the supplier is in delay or if tests were unfairly applied;  
  - decide whether non‑conformity is material;  
  - decide whether the buyer’s withholding and termination were lawful;  
  - award damages or order specific performance (subject to enforceability constraints).

### c) Interim measures and payments pending arbitration

If a dispute arises and arbitration is invoked:

- The buyer may continue to **withhold contested payments** provided it has a good‑faith basis and follows the contract;  
- The supplier may seek:
  - **interim measures** from the tribunal (or the courts in support of arbitration) to secure payment or preserve assets; or  
  - a **partial award** on undisputed sums.

UAE courts generally do **not** re‑examine the merits if there is a valid arbitration agreement but may assist with **interim relief**, **evidence**, and **enforcement** of the award.

---

## 8. Applying this to your scenario (high‑level)

Given your fact pattern:

- **Late delivery**:  
  – assess whether contract makes time of the essence, provides LDs, and defines long‑stop dates;  
  – prolonged delay strengthens buyer’s case for termination or LDs.

- **Failed acceptance tests**:  
  – if tests are objectively defined and repeatedly failed, that supports a **non‑conformity** / fundamental breach argument;  
  – ensure all test results and notices are well documented.

- **Withheld final payment**:  
  – if final payment is expressly linked to successful acceptance, withholding is likely defensible under UAE law, provided the buyer has not accepted the goods and has clearly notified reasons.

- **Buyer termination**:  
  – legality depends on:
    - whether contractual termination preconditions (notice, cure periods, thresholds) were strictly followed; and  
    - whether the supplier’s breach is “serious” enough under UAE standards.  
  – if termination was premature (e.g., no cure opportunity), the supplier might claim wrongful termination.

- **Supplier claim of “substantial compliance” and threat of arbitration**:  
  – this will turn on technical evidence:
    - did the equipment meet the contractual performance specs, or are the deviations material?  
    - was the testing process itself contract‑compliant and fair?

An arbitral tribunal applying UAE law will weigh:

- contract wording (especially on tests, acceptance, LDs, termination);  
- chronological record of delay, test failures, notices and responses;  
- expert evidence on technical performance and causation;  
- whether the buyer’s withholding and termination were proportionate and procedurally compliant.

---

If you’d like, I can help you:

- map your actual contract clauses (delay, tests, payment, termination, LDs, arbitration) against these UAE‑law principles, or  
- draft a **position paper / memo** outlining buyer‑side or supplier‑side arguments for a potential arbitration.

INSPECTION, TESTING, ACCEPTANCE, WITHHOLDING AND TERMINATION FOR CAUSE

1. Definitions

1.1 In this Agreement, and in this Clause, the following terms shall have the meanings set out below:

(a) “Equipment” means the equipment, materials, components, software (if any), and associated documentation to be supplied by the Supplier under this Agreement, as further described in the Specifications.

(b) “Specifications” means the technical specifications, performance criteria, functional requirements, drawings, standards, and any other requirements expressly set out in this Agreement, its schedules and annexes, and any agreed written variations thereto.

(c) “Delivery Date” means the date or dates for delivery of the Equipment as specified in this Agreement, as may be amended in accordance with its terms.

(d) “Inspection” means the review, examination and verification activities carried out by or on behalf of the Buyer to determine whether the Equipment conforms to the Specifications and the Agreement, including visual inspection, document review and such other checks as the Buyer reasonably deems necessary.

(e) “Tests” or “Acceptance Tests” means the tests, trials and demonstrations described in this Agreement and/or the Specifications, to be carried out to determine whether the Equipment meets the Specifications, including performance, reliability, safety and integration requirements.

(f) “Acceptance” means the Buyer’s written confirmation that the Equipment has successfully passed all required Inspections and Acceptance Tests and meets all applicable requirements of this Agreement, subject only to any minor defects expressly agreed in writing by the Buyer to be remedied after Acceptance.

(g) “Substantial Compliance” or “Substantial Performance” means, for the purposes of this Agreement only, performance that meets all material requirements of the Specifications and this Agreement so that the Equipment is fully fit for its intended purpose, with only minor defects which do not affect safety, functionality, performance, reliability, serviceability, or integration with the Buyer’s systems, and which can be remedied without material disruption to the Buyer’s operations. The existence of any material non-conformity shall exclude any claim by the Supplier of Substantial Compliance or Substantial Performance.

(h) “Non-Conformity” means any failure of the Equipment to comply with the Specifications, this Agreement, applicable law, good industry practice, or any failure to successfully pass any Inspection or Acceptance Test.

(i) “Cure Period” has the meaning given in Clause 6.3 below.

2. Inspection and Testing

2.1 Right to Inspect and Witness Tests

(a) The Buyer, its employees, agents, and/or representatives shall have the right, but not the obligation, to:
   (i) inspect the Equipment, any components, and related documentation at the Supplier’s premises, at the premises of any sub-supplier, and/or at the Delivery Location; and
   (ii) witness any factory tests, pre‑shipment tests, site tests, commissioning tests, and Acceptance Tests,

in each case upon reasonable prior notice and during normal working hours, provided that such activities do not unreasonably disrupt the Supplier’s operations.

(b) The Supplier shall provide the Buyer with all reasonable assistance, access, information, and documentation requested for the purposes of Inspection and witnessing tests, including test procedures, test plans, test records, and calibration certificates.

2.2 Test Procedures, Criteria and Schedule

(a) The parties shall agree in writing, prior to commencement of any Acceptance Test, the detailed test procedures, acceptance criteria, and test schedule, consistent with the Specifications and the provisions of this Agreement. In the event of any inconsistency, the stricter or more demanding requirement shall apply, unless the parties expressly agree otherwise in writing.

(b) The Supplier shall give the Buyer not less than [●] Business Days’ prior written notice of the date on which any Test(s) will be carried out, and shall not proceed with any Test that the Buyer has reasonably requested be rescheduled, provided that such rescheduling does not result in an unreasonable delay.

2.3 Costs of Testing

(a) The Supplier shall bear all costs of Inspections and Tests conducted at its own or its sub‑suppliers’ premises, including provision of necessary equipment, materials, consumables, utilities and personnel.

(b) The Supplier shall bear all costs of any re‑tests required due to Non‑Conformity or failure to pass any Test. If the Buyer incurs any reasonable additional costs as a direct result of such re‑tests (including travel and accommodation of its representatives), the Supplier shall reimburse those costs upon presentation of reasonable supporting documentation.

3. Delivery, Late Delivery and Consequences

3.1 Timely Delivery

(a) Time for delivery of the Equipment in accordance with the Delivery Date(s) is of the essence of this Agreement.

(b) The Supplier shall deliver the Equipment in accordance with the agreed Incoterms, Delivery Date(s), and any delivery requirements set out in this Agreement.

3.2 Notice of Delay

(a) The Supplier shall promptly notify the Buyer in writing as soon as it becomes aware of any circumstance likely to cause a delay in delivery or completion of Tests or Acceptance. Such notice shall set out:
   (i) the cause of the delay;
   (ii) the expected duration of the delay; and
   (iii) proposed measures to mitigate the delay.

(b) The giving of such notice shall not relieve the Supplier of any of its obligations or liabilities under this Agreement, nor shall it constitute a waiver by the Buyer of any rights or remedies.

3.3 Consequences of Late Delivery

(a) Without prejudice to any other rights or remedies of the Buyer (including liquidated damages, if provided elsewhere in this Agreement), if the Supplier fails to deliver the Equipment by the relevant Delivery Date, the Buyer shall be entitled, at its option, to:
   (i) accept late delivery, subject to any applicable liquidated damages or other remedies; and/or
   (ii) withhold any payments linked to delivery and/or Acceptance until such time as full delivery and Acceptance are achieved; and/or
   (iii) treat such delay as a material breach for the purpose of termination under Clause 6 below, if the delay exceeds [●] days or such other period as may be specified in this Agreement.

4. Acceptance Procedure

4.1 Delivery, Installation and Commissioning

(a) Upon delivery of the Equipment to the Delivery Location, the Supplier shall, where applicable, install and commission the Equipment in accordance with the Agreement, the Specifications, and good industry practice.

(b) The Supplier shall notify the Buyer in writing when the Equipment is ready for Acceptance Testing.

4.2 Conduct of Acceptance Tests

(a) The Buyer shall commence Acceptance Tests within [●] Business Days after receipt of the Supplier’s notice under Clause 4.1(b), or such other period as the parties may agree in writing.

(b) Acceptance Tests shall be conducted in accordance with the agreed test procedures and criteria. The Buyer may, acting reasonably, require additional or extended tests where necessary to confirm compliance with the Specifications or to verify the rectification of any Non-Conformity.

4.3 Acceptance or Rejection

(a) Within [●] Business Days after completion of the Acceptance Tests, the Buyer shall notify the Supplier in writing of:
   (i) its Acceptance of the Equipment; or
   (ii) its rejection of the Equipment, specifying in reasonable detail any Non-Conformities identified.

(b) If the Buyer does not issue a notification within the period referred to in Clause 4.3(a), and provided that:
   (i) the Supplier has given written notice that the Equipment is ready for Acceptance Testing; and
   (ii) the Buyer has had a reasonable opportunity to perform Acceptance Tests; and
   (iii) there are no unresolved Non‑Conformities previously notified by the Buyer;
then the Equipment shall not be deemed accepted solely by reason of the passage of time, but the Supplier may request in writing that the Buyer promptly complete the Acceptance Tests. The parties shall then agree a short, reasonable period within which such Tests shall be completed. Any deemed acceptance must be expressly agreed in writing by the Buyer; silence or non‑response shall not constitute Acceptance.

4.4 Effect of Acceptance; No Waiver of Latent Defects

(a) Acceptance of the Equipment confirms only that, at the time of Acceptance, the Equipment met the Acceptance criteria then tested. Acceptance does not:
   (i) constitute a waiver of any latent or hidden defects; or
   (ii) limit or exclude the Supplier’s obligations or liabilities under warranties, guarantees, or other provisions of this Agreement.

(b) The Buyer shall be entitled to notify the Supplier of any latent or hidden Non‑Conformity discovered after Acceptance and to require the Supplier to remedy such Non‑Conformity in accordance with the warranty provisions of this Agreement.

5. Substantial Compliance and Non‑Conformities

5.1 Substantial Compliance

(a) The Supplier acknowledges and agrees that:
   (i) “Substantial Compliance” or “Substantial Performance” shall have the limited meaning set out in Clause 1.1(g); and
   (ii) any decision as to whether the Equipment meets the threshold of Substantial Compliance shall be made by the Buyer acting reasonably and in good faith, having regard to the Specifications and the intended purpose of the Equipment.

(b) For avoidance of doubt, the Supplier shall not be entitled to claim that the Buyer is obliged to accept the Equipment solely on the basis of partial, incomplete or approximate performance, or on grounds of Substantial Compliance, where:
   (i) the Equipment does not fully meet all material requirements of the Specifications; or
   (ii) the Equipment fails any material Acceptance Test; or
   (iii) any Non-Conformity adversely affects safety, functionality, performance, reliability, compatibility or regulatory compliance.

5.2 Minor Defects

(a) The Buyer may, but is not obliged to, grant Acceptance subject to the Supplier’s written agreement to remedy minor defects within a specified time. Minor defects are those that:
   (i) do not affect safety;
   (ii) do not materially affect functionality, performance, or reliability; and
   (iii) can be remedied without material impact on the Buyer’s operations.

(b) Any list of minor defects and their agreed rectification period shall be set out in an agreed punch list signed by both parties. The Supplier shall promptly remedy all such minor defects at its own cost within the period specified, failing which the Buyer may exercise its rights under Clauses 5.3 and 6.

5.3 Failed Tests and Repeated Non-Conformities

(a) If the Equipment fails any Acceptance Test or is otherwise found to be Non-Conforming, the Buyer may reject the Equipment in whole or in part and require the Supplier, at the Supplier’s sole cost and risk and within a time period reasonably specified by the Buyer, to:
   (i) promptly remedy the Non-Conformity; and/or
   (ii) replace the Non‑Conforming Equipment with new conforming equipment; and/or
   (iii) repeat the relevant Tests after correction or replacement.

(b) If, after the Supplier’s remedial efforts, the Equipment again fails any Acceptance Test, or if the Supplier fails to remedy the Non-Conformity within the specified time:
   (i) the Buyer may, at its sole discretion and without prejudice to any other rights and remedies, elect one or more of the following:
       (A) allow the Supplier a further opportunity to remedy the Non-Conformity under a revised timetable agreed in writing; or
       (B) procure alternative equipment and/or services from a third party and recover from the Supplier all additional direct costs reasonably incurred by the Buyer as a result; or
       (C) reject the Equipment in whole or in part and terminate this Agreement, in whole or in part, for cause under Clause 6; and
   (ii) the Supplier shall refund to the Buyer all amounts paid in respect of any rejected Equipment, together with any associated charges, within [●] days of the Buyer’s written demand.

6. Withholding of Payments

6.1 Milestone‑Linked Payments

(a) Where payments are linked to delivery milestones, completion of Tests, and/or Acceptance, the Supplier acknowledges that the Buyer is under no obligation to make such payments unless and until the relevant milestone has been properly achieved and documented.

(b) The Supplier shall submit invoices only for milestones that have been achieved in accordance with this Agreement. The Buyer shall be entitled to reject any invoice that does not correspond to an achieved milestone.

6.2 Right to Withhold

(a) Without prejudice to any other rights or remedies, the Buyer may withhold payment of any portion of the Contract Price which corresponds to:
   (i) Equipment that has not been delivered in accordance with this Agreement;
   (ii) Equipment that has not been Accepted in accordance with Clause 4;
   (iii) portions of work or Equipment affected by a notified Non-Conformity;
   (iv) any amounts reasonably disputed by the Buyer in good faith; or
   (v) any amounts that the Buyer is entitled to set off under this Agreement.

(b) The Buyer shall notify the Supplier in writing of its reasons for withholding any payment, and, to the extent reasonably practicable, the amount so withheld shall be proportionate to the value of the Non‑Conforming or undelivered Equipment or the disputed amount.

6.3 Cure of Non‑Conformity and Release of Withheld Amounts

(a) Where payment has been withheld due to Non‑Conformity or failure to achieve a milestone, the Supplier shall remedy the cause of withholding within a period to be specified by the Buyer in writing (the “Cure Period”), taking into account the nature and seriousness of the issue.

(b) Once the Supplier has remedied the Non‑Conformity and the Equipment has successfully passed any required re‑Tests and/or has been Accepted, the Buyer shall pay any withheld amounts that are no longer in dispute within [●] days, subject always to:
   (i) the Buyer’s right of set‑off against any sums due to the Buyer from the Supplier; and
   (ii) any other rights and remedies that the Buyer may have under this Agreement or at law.

(c) The Supplier acknowledges that the Buyer’s withholding of payment in accordance with this Clause 6 shall not constitute a breach of this Agreement, nor entitle the Supplier to suspend performance or to terminate this Agreement, provided that the Buyer acts in good faith.

7. Termination for Cause

7.1 Buyer’s Right to Terminate for Cause

Without prejudice to any other rights or remedies available under this Agreement, at law or in equity, the Buyer may, by written notice to the Supplier, terminate this Agreement in whole or in part with immediate effect (or with effect from such date as the Buyer may specify in the notice) upon the occurrence of any of the following events:

(a) Material Delay:
   The Supplier fails to deliver the Equipment, or any material portion thereof, within [●] days after the applicable Delivery Date, or fails to achieve Acceptance within [●] days after the date originally scheduled for Acceptance, other than due to a force majeure event duly notified in accordance with this Agreement.

(b) Repeated Failure of Tests:
   The Equipment fails any material Acceptance Test on [●] or more occasions, or repeated Non‑Conformities occur which, in the reasonable opinion of the Buyer, indicate that the Supplier is unable or unwilling to provide conforming Equipment within a reasonable time.

(c) Failure to Remedy:
   The Supplier fails to remedy any Non‑Conformity or other material breach relating to delivery, quality, performance, or Testing of the Equipment within the applicable Cure Period specified in a written notice from the Buyer.

(d) Persistent Breach:
   The Supplier commits repeated, persistent or systemic breaches of its obligations under this Agreement (whether or not remedied) which, taken together, materially impair the achievement of the purpose of this Agreement or the Buyer’s ability to use the Equipment as intended.

(e) Insolvency or Similar Events:
   Any insolvency, bankruptcy, liquidation, or comparable event occurs in respect of the Supplier, as further described in the general termination provisions of this Agreement.

7.2 Procedure and Consequences of Termination for Cause

(a) The Buyer shall notify the Supplier in writing of its decision to terminate under Clause 7.1, specifying the grounds for termination and the effective date of termination.

(b) Upon termination for cause pursuant to this Clause 7:
   (i) the Supplier shall immediately cease all affected work and shall take all necessary steps to protect and preserve the Equipment, materials and any items belonging to the Buyer;
   (ii) the Buyer may take over any partially completed Equipment, materials, documentation, and work‑in‑progress, and may use them to complete the project itself or to have a third party do so; and
   (iii) the Supplier shall promptly refund to the Buyer all amounts paid in respect of Equipment which has not been delivered and Accepted in accordance with this Agreement, together with any other amounts refundable under this Agreement.

(c) The Buyer shall be entitled to recover from the Supplier all direct additional costs and expenses reasonably incurred by the Buyer in procuring substitute equipment and/or services from a third party as a result of such termination, subject to any agreed limitations of liability under this Agreement.

7.3 Effect on Substantial Compliance Claims

(a) Termination by the Buyer under this Clause 7 shall not be affected by, nor conditional upon, any claim by the Supplier that it has achieved Substantial Compliance or Substantial Performance.

(b) Any dispute as to whether the Supplier has achieved Substantial Compliance or Substantial Performance shall not limit or delay the Buyer’s right to terminate under this Clause 7, provided that the Buyer has acted reasonably and in good faith in assessing the Supplier’s performance.

8. Reservation of Rights

8.1 The rights and remedies of the Buyer under this Clause are cumulative and are in addition to, and not in substitution for, any other rights or remedies available to the Buyer under this Agreement, under applicable law (including the laws of the United Arab Emirates), or otherwise.

8.2 No failure or delay by the Buyer in exercising any right, power or remedy shall operate as a waiver thereof, nor shall any single or partial exercise of any such right, power or remedy preclude any other or further exercise thereof or the exercise of any other right, power or remedy.
